name: Biere de Garde
title: Biere de Garde: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Biere de Garde explained: the malty, cellar aged farmhouse ale of northern France. Flavour, serving, Indian food pairings and availability.
tagline: The farmhouse beer that was brewed in winter and kept for the summer harvest.
tastes:
Biere de garde means beer for keeping. Farm breweries in French Flanders, on the border with Belgium, brewed it in the cooler months and held it in cellars for the warm season when brewing was risky. That long, cold rest is what shapes it: the beer comes out smooth and rounded, with the rough edges of fermentation worn away.

Expect a malt led beer. The common versions are amber or brown, with toffee, bread crust and a faint cellar earthiness some drinkers call musty in a good way. Blond versions exist and are a little drier and spicier. Hops stay in the background, a herbal note rather than a bitter one. Strength runs from table beer to something closer to a strong ale, so read the label.

What separates it from a Belgian saison is restraint. Saison is peppery, dry and yeast driven. Biere de garde is clean, malty and patient, often fermented with ale yeast at the cool end or with lager yeast, then lagered for weeks. It is a beer for the table more than the bar.

profile.look: Gold, amber or chestnut, mostly clear, with a lasting off white head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Toffee, toast and bread crust, a light herbal hop, an earthy cellar note, very little fruity yeast character.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium body, smooth and rounded from long conditioning, moderate carbonation, a dry enough finish for food.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner and Vienna or Munich malts, some caramel malt for amber versions, French or German noble hops, clean ale or lager yeast.

in_india: A beer built for keeping suits a country where beer often sits in a warehouse longer than the brewer would like. It still needs cold storage, but the malty profile hides age better than a hop led beer. The catch is time: weeks of lagering ties up tanks, which is why Indian brewpubs rarely make it. Open a bottle at a long family lunch rather than a hot afternoon.

pairings.why: Toffee malt meets the smoky, buttery gravy and the dry finish resets the palate between bites.
The earthy, malty beer softens the vinegar and spice without fighting them.
Roasted coconut and poppy seed echo the bread crust malt.
Caramel malt and cooked carrot, ghee and milk solids share the same browned sweetness.

examples_note: We could not find a verified Indian commercial example. A brewpub with spare tank time is your best chance, so ask.
